title: OpenAI to Launch Major PR Push: Renaming Data Centers as AI Compute Parks
excerpt: A public relations offensive aimed at Washington and voters is taking shape inside OpenAI. According to Axios, the company plans to launch a large-scale campaig
content_html:
A public relations offensive aimed at Washington and voters is taking shape inside OpenAI. According to Axios, the company plans to launch a large-scale campaign once this Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections are over. The person behind it is Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane, and his read is blunt: the midterms are merely a "trailer" for the 2028 presidential election, and AI is destined to become a central issue on the campaign stage. With regulation and public opinion both tightening, getting ahead to define the narrative has become a defensive battle this company has no choice but to fight.

From Tech Product to Political Issue

Lehane revealed that OpenAI will step up its AI outreach to the public. Its playbook has several moves: while discussing setting speed limits on AI development, it is also looking for ways to make ordinary people genuinely feel how AI improves daily life; at the same time, it is pushing for the United States to lead global standards-setting. Framing AI as moving from "technology in the lab" to "national competitiveness and lifestyle" is the core shift in this narrative push—it no longer just wants to sell models, but also wants to win the power to shape public opinion and policy. For a giant that holds frontier models and is mired in controversies over compute and electricity use, proactively steering the conversation toward "empowerment" is clearly more advantageous than passively taking criticism.

Rebranding Data Centers

The most interesting move is repackaging "data centers" as "AI compute parks." Previously, this kind of mega-infrastructure frequently sparked protests over land use, power consumption, and community disruption; Amazon and Microsoft have both said they will no longer use nondisclosure agreements when discussing projects with local governments. OpenAI clearly wants to use the new label to soften the impression of a "Big Tech land grab" and frame the controversy as a "good and healthy conversation." When compute becomes a bargaining chip in votes and geopolitical competition, the center of gravity for tech company PR shifts from product launches to city halls and televised debates.
